name: Getting started with GGLearn
description: Find your path, take your first exam, earn your first certificate.

groups.quest: daily quest, XP or streak term

cards.subject: A track
says: is one subject, product, service, tool, technology or process you can learn
has its own ladder of 20 levels
is the unit you join and sit exams in
cards.use: want to know what you choose when you decide what to learn
not: is a single exam question

cards.subject: A level
says: is one step on a track's ladder of 20
is passed by sitting an exam
opens the next step once you pass it
cards.use: want to know what you pass to move forward
not: is a whole subject on its own

cards.subject: Novice
says: is the name of level 1
starts every track's ladder
is where a new learner begins unless a placement check puts them higher
cards.use: need the name of the bottom step of a track
not: is the name of the top level

cards.subject: Titan
says: is the name of level 20
sits at the top of every track's ladder
is also the name of the certificate for level 20
cards.use: need the name of the top step of a track
not: is the name of level 1

cards.subject: Level unlocking
says: lets you start a level only after passing the one before it
keeps the levels in a fixed order
is why you cannot jump from level 4 straight to level 6
cards.use: wonder why you cannot take a later exam yet
not: lets you take any level at any time

cards.subject: The study guide
says: shows a level's syllabus before its exam
contains flip cards for the level
counts as a daily quest when you read it
cards.use: want to prepare for a level before its exam
not: shows the exact questions of your next exam

cards.subject: A flip card
says: turns a key point of a level into a quick question-and-answer prompt
is drawn from the questions of that level
lives inside the study guide
cards.use: want a quick way to revise a level's key points
not: is a printed certificate

cards.subject: The syllabus
says: lists what a level covers
tells you what to learn before the level exam
opens the study guide for each level
cards.use: need to know which topics a level will test
not: lists your rival's answers

cards.subject: The dashboard
says: lists tracks you are required to take under Required for you
shows due dates for required tracks
compares your levels with your rival's
cards.use: want one place to see what you should do next
not: is where you change your password only

cards.subject: A required track
says: is assigned to you with a due date
appears on the dashboard under Required for you
shows as overdue once its due date has passed
cards.use: see a track that has a deadline attached
not: can be ignored until after its due date

cards.subject: A customer track
says: is a track made for customers
is the only kind a customer account can open
keeps staff-only tracks out of a customer's view
cards.use: wonder why some tracks do not appear on your account
not: is open to every account regardless of audience

cards.subject: A track goal
says: is the aim you record when you join a track
belongs to you for that one track
gives your study a target to work towards
cards.use: want to decide how far to climb on a track
not: is chosen by your rival

cards.subject: The level exam
says: asks up to 10 questions
is how a level is passed
follows the study guide for that level
cards.use: want to know how you pass a level
not: lasts a fixed three hours

cards.subject: The pass mark
says: is 80%
must be reached for a level to count as passed
lets you miss two questions out of ten and still pass
cards.use: need the score that passes a level exam
not: is 50%

cards.subject: A fresh draw
says: selects a different set of questions on each attempt
favours questions you have not yet answered correctly
stops you memorising one fixed paper
cards.use: wonder why your second attempt looked different
not: gives every attempt exactly the same questions

cards.subject: A retake
says: is allowed after a failed exam
leaves the level locked until you pass
does not lock you out for a waiting period
cards.use: have just failed a level exam
not: removes you from the track

cards.subject: Automatic marking
says: checks multiple-choice answers against the answer key
needs no human grader
returns your result as soon as you finish
cards.use: wonder who marks the multiple-choice questions
not: is done by a vote of other learners

cards.subject: Rubric marking
says: grades open and scenario answers against a reference answer
rewards covering the key points a good answer should include
does not reward length for its own sake
cards.use: wonder how a written answer gets its score
not: gives every written answer the same score

cards.subject: The keyword fallback
says: is a coarse check used when AI marking is unavailable
looks for the expected words in a written answer
is cruder than rubric marking
cards.use: hear that written answers can be checked without AI
not: replaces automatic marking for multiple-choice questions

cards.subject: A multiple-choice question
says: presents several options of which one is correct
is marked automatically
asks you to pick rather than write
cards.use: face a question with options a to d
not: asks for a written paragraph

cards.subject: An open question
says: asks for a written answer in your own words
is marked against a rubric
cannot be answered by picking from options
cards.use: face a question that wants a written answer
not: is marked by counting your characters

cards.subject: A scenario question
says: describes a realistic situation and asks what you would do
is graded against a reference answer and rubric
tests applying knowledge rather than recalling a fact
cards.use: face a question that begins with a short story
not: asks only for a definition

cards.subject: A certificate
says: is issued when you pass level 5, 10, 15 or 20
carries a public code
comes in four kinds
cards.use: want to know what you earn at the milestone levels
not: is issued after every level you pass

cards.subject: The Foundation certificate
says: is issued on passing level 5
is the first of the four certificates
marks the first milestone on a track
cards.use: need the certificate for level 5
not: is issued on passing level 10

cards.subject: The Practitioner certificate
says: is issued on passing level 10
sits between Foundation and Expert
marks the halfway milestone
cards.use: need the certificate for level 10
not: is issued on passing level 20

cards.subject: The Expert certificate
says: is issued on passing level 15
comes after Practitioner
is the last milestone before Titan
cards.use: need the certificate for level 15
not: is issued on passing level 5

cards.subject: The Titan certificate
says: is issued on passing level 20
is the highest of the four certificates
completes a track's ladder
cards.use: need the certificate for the top level
not: is issued on passing level 15

cards.subject: A milestone level
says: is one of levels 5, 10, 15 and 20
issues a certificate when passed
is spaced every five levels
cards.use: want to know which levels reward you with a certificate
not: is any level you pass

cards.subject: A certificate code
says: is a public code on each certificate
lets anyone confirm the certificate is genuine
is checked at /cert/ followed by the code
cards.use: need to prove a certificate is real
not: can only be checked by phoning the learner

cards.subject: The placement check
says: is a short set of questions
finds the level you already know
lets you start above level 1
cards.use: already know a subject and want to skip the basics
not: resets all your progress

cards.subject: The placement ceiling
says: never places anyone past level 15
means levels above 15 have to be earned by exam
applies even when every placement answer is right
cards.use: wonder how high the placement check can start you
not: lets you start at level 20 if you score perfectly

cards.subject: A daily quest
says: is one of three small tasks offered on each track every day
earns XP when completed
counts toward your streak
cards.use: want to know what to do each day on a track
not: is a monthly exam

cards.subject: The study-guide quest
says: is earned by reading the study guide
pays 20 XP
is the smallest of the three quest rewards
cards.use: want the quest that pays 20 XP
not: pays 40 XP

cards.subject: The drill quest
says: is earned by answering a five-question drill
pays 30 XP
gives instant feedback on each answer
cards.use: want the quest that pays 30 XP
not: is a three-hour timed exam

cards.subject: The exam quest
says: is earned by finishing any level exam
pays 40 XP
pays the most of the three quests
cards.use: want the quest that pays 40 XP
not: pays 20 XP

cards.subject: XP
says: measures effort from quests and exams
feeds your race with your rival
has no cash value
cards.use: wonder what the points on your dashboard mean
not: can be withdrawn as money

cards.subject: A streak
says: counts consecutive days with at least one quest completed
must end today or yesterday to count
resets after a missed day
cards.use: want to know how a streak is counted
not: counts total days since you joined

cards.subject: The drill question pool
says: draws only from levels you have already passed
starts at level 1 for a brand-new learner
never reveals the exam you are about to sit
cards.use: wonder which questions a drill uses
not: draws from the level you are about to sit

cards.subject: A rival
says: is a named opponent on each track
earns XP every day
stays the same rival for a given track
cards.use: want to know who you are racing on a track
not: is another customer's account

cards.subject: The rival scale
says: treats 150 XP as one level
turns a rival's XP into a level
lets the dashboard compare your levels with your rival's
cards.use: need to convert a rival's XP into a level
not: treats 15 XP as one level

cards.subject: A badge
says: marks a milestone such as passing your first level
includes a 3-day and a 7-day streak
includes earning a certificate
cards.use: want to know what rewards a milestone
not: is a payment

cards.subject: An unfinished quest day
says: still shows yesterday's streak while today is not over
lets you keep the streak by completing a quest before the day ends
loses the streak only if the day passes with no quest
cards.use: opened GGLearn in the morning before doing a quest
not: resets your streak at the moment you log in

cards.subject: A contest
says: is a time-boxed race on one track
is decided by who gains levels
lets people race against each other
cards.use: want to compete with others on a track
not: is a single exam question

cards.subject: The contest goal
says: is a number of levels to gain, from 1 to 20
defines what reaching the finish means
is measured in levels, not hours studied
cards.use: need the target a contest runner must reach
not: is a number of exams to retake

cards.subject: The contest deadline
says: lasts from 1 to 90 days
ends the race
ends the race for every player at once
cards.use: need to know how long a contest can run
not: can be up to a year

cards.subject: Growth-based progress
says: counts levels gained rather than levels held
lets beginners and experts race fairly
gives an expert's high starting level no head start
cards.use: wonder why a contest suits both beginners and experts
not: ranks players by their level at the start

cards.subject: Contest ranking
says: puts first whoever reached the goal first
breaks ties by levels gained
puts total XP only after goal time and levels gained
cards.use: need to know who wins a contest
not: goes to whoever has the highest starting level

cards.subject: The organiser
says: runs a contest and invites people
pays any cash prize
arranges payment of winners directly
cards.use: want to know who sets up and pays for a contest
not: is paid by GGLearn to hold the prize

cards.subject: A private contest
says: can be opened only by the organiser, invited people and members
shows everyone else a not-found page
keeps your name and progress out of public view
cards.use: want a race that outsiders cannot watch
not: can be watched by anyone

cards.subject: A public contest
says: can be watched by anyone
requires your consent before you join
makes your name, photo and progress public
cards.use: want a race that anyone can watch
not: hides you from every stranger

cards.subject: A simulated bot
says: follows a fixed daily XP schedule
is labelled as simulated
does not study or answer questions
cards.use: see a contest entry marked as simulated
not: answers exam questions like a learner

cards.subject: A cash prize
says: is optional
is paid by the organiser to winners
is never held or moved by GGLearn
cards.use: wonder who pays when a contest offers money
not: is paid out of a fund GGLearn holds

cards.subject: The XP window
says: is the period between the contest start and its deadline
counts only XP earned inside it
is the last tie-breaker in the ranking
cards.use: need to know which XP counts as a final tie-breaker
not: counts all XP you ever earned

cards.subject: An invite link
says: is how you get a GGLearn account
is single-use
is tied to one email address
cards.use: want to know how a person gets an account
not: lets anyone sign up from the home page

cards.subject: Invite expiry
says: falls 7 days after the link is issued
makes an old link invalid
is fixed by asking for a new link
cards.use: find that a link no longer works after a week
not: never happens

cards.subject: A used invite
says: cannot be opened a second time
shows as not valid
has to be replaced with a new link
cards.use: try the same link twice
not: can be reused as often as you like

cards.subject: The invite email
says: is the one address an invite works for
means a forwarded link does not work for someone else
must be the address the organisation used when inviting you
cards.use: forward your invite to a colleague
not: can be changed by whoever holds the link

cards.subject: The password minimum
says: is 8 characters or more
applies when you set your password
is a floor, not a recommendation for a good password
cards.use: need the shortest allowed GGLearn password
not: is 4 characters

cards.subject: A strong password
says: is long and not used anywhere else
is better as a passphrase than as a short complicated word
does not contain your name or birth year
cards.use: need to choose a password that is hard to guess
not: is your name followed by 1

cards.subject: A password manager
says: generates and stores a different password for every site
removes the need to remember each one
fills in only on the site it was saved for
cards.use: want a different strong password everywhere without memorising them
not: works by reusing one password everywhere

cards.subject: A reused password
says: lets one breached site expose your other accounts
is the main reason to use a different password on each site
turns one leak into many
cards.use: hear that one site you use has been breached
not: is safe as long as it is long

cards.subject: A profile photo
says: is optional
can be a JPEG, PNG or WebP
must be 300 KB or smaller
cards.use: want to add a picture to your account
not: must be a GIF

cards.subject: Photo visibility
says: lets signed-in colleagues see your photo
shows strangers your photo only when you play in a public contest
is limited by default
cards.use: wonder who can see your picture
not: makes your photo visible to everyone online

cards.subject: Sign out everywhere
says: ends your session on every device
is the right move on a shared or lost device
is more thorough than closing one tab
cards.use: may have left yourself signed in on a computer you cannot reach
not: only signs you out of this browser

cards.subject: A shared computer
says: keeps your session open after you close the tab unless you sign out
is the place most likely to leave you signed in by mistake
is a reason never to tick remember me
cards.use: are using a library or office computer
not: signs you out automatically when the tab closes

cards.subject: A phishing message
says: imitates a trusted sender to collect your password
urges you to act at once
is best met by going to the site directly rather than the link
cards.use: get an email saying your account locks in an hour
not: is safe to answer with your password

cards.subject: Retrieval practice
says: means recalling an answer from memory instead of rereading
strengthens memory more than rereading
is what a drill with instant feedback asks of you
cards.use: want a study method that builds lasting memory
not: means reading the same page again

cards.subject: Spaced practice
says: spreads study over several sessions
beats the same time crammed into one sitting
lets you revisit material just as it begins to fade
cards.use: have three weeks before an exam
not: packs all study into one long session

cards.subject: Cramming
says: packs all study into one long session just before a test
feels productive but is forgotten quickly
is the opposite of spaced practice
cards.use: are tempted to study everything the night before
not: builds the strongest long-term memory

cards.subject: Interleaving
says: mixes different topics in one session
feels harder than blocked practice but helps later
trains you to tell similar ideas apart
cards.use: want to avoid studying one topic at a time for hours
not: repeats one topic until it feels easy

cards.subject: Blocked practice
says: repeats one topic until it feels easy
gives a false sense of mastery
is the usual alternative to interleaving
cards.use: notice you keep drilling a single topic
not: mixes topics randomly

cards.subject: The forgetting curve
says: shows memory fading fast after learning and then more slowly
is flattened by each well-timed review
is the reason review is better than one big session
cards.use: wonder why you forget material within days
not: shows memory staying constant after learning

cards.subject: Elaboration
says: asks you to explain why something is true
links new facts to what you already know
turns a bare fact into connected understanding
cards.use: want to understand rather than memorise a rule
not: means copying a definition word for word

cards.subject: Chunking
says: groups items into meaningful units
makes long lists easier to hold in working memory
is why a phone number is split into groups
cards.use: need to remember a long list of steps
not: means studying in short sessions

cards.subject: A mnemonic
says: is a memory aid such as a rhyme or an acronym
works best for lists and fixed orders
turns an abstract item into something memorable
cards.use: need to remember an ordered list
not: replaces understanding the topic

cards.subject: Dual coding
says: combines words with a picture or diagram
gives memory two routes to the same idea
helps most with processes and structures
cards.use: want to remember a process with several parts
not: means studying in two languages

cards.subject: Desirable difficulty
says: makes learning slightly harder on purpose
improves long-term retention even though it feels slower
includes testing yourself before you feel ready
cards.use: wonder why harder practice helps more than easy practice
not: means choosing the hardest material available

cards.subject: Sleep consolidation
says: stabilises new memories during sleep
is why a night of sleep after studying helps
is undermined by an all-nighter
cards.use: are deciding between sleeping and a late-night cram
not: happens only while you are awake

cards.subject: Working memory
says: holds only a few items at a time
is overloaded by too much new material at once
is why small study chunks work better
cards.use: feel overwhelmed by too much new content in one go
not: has unlimited capacity

cards.subject: The generation effect
says: makes you remember an answer better when you produced it yourself
explains why attempting a question before looking helps
favours trying first over reading the answer
cards.use: want to know why guessing before you check improves memory
not: says that reading the answer first is best

cards.subject: A short daily session
says: beats one long weekly session
keeps material fresh
fits the daily quest rhythm
cards.use: have limited time but can study every day
not: works only if it lasts two hours

cards.subject: A fixed study time
says: ties studying to a set time of day
removes the daily decision about when to start
makes the habit easier to keep
cards.use: keep putting off when to study
not: relies on feeling motivated

cards.subject: Reading the syllabus first
says: shows what an exam will cover before you study
stops you spending time on the wrong topics
gives your session a clear target
cards.use: are about to start preparing for a level
not: comes after the exam

cards.subject: A mistake card
says: turns a question you missed into a card to review
targets your weakest points
is rewritten in your own words
cards.use: keep missing the same question
not: records only the questions you got right

cards.subject: Teaching it back
says: means explaining the topic to someone without notes
exposes gaps you did not know you had
is a form of retrieval practice
cards.use: want to test whether you really understand a topic
not: means reading your notes aloud

cards.subject: Exam-condition practice
says: uses a timer and no notes
shows how you perform under pressure
builds familiarity with the real exam
cards.use: want to rehearse before a level exam
not: lets you look up answers as you go

cards.subject: Reviewing wrong answers
says: means working out why each wrong answer was wrong
turns a miss into learning
is worth more than moving straight on
cards.use: just got feedback on a drill
not: means ignoring the questions you missed

cards.subject: Your own summary
says: puts a topic in your own words
is better than copying the text
shows what you do and do not understand
cards.use: want a short revision sheet for a level
not: is a copy of the study guide

cards.subject: A timed focus block
says: alternates short focused work with short breaks
protects concentration
makes starting easier because the end is in sight
cards.use: find your attention fades after a while
not: means working for hours without a break

cards.subject: Removing distractions
says: means putting the phone away and turning notifications off
protects focus during a session
is easier to do before you start than during
cards.use: get pulled away from studying by notifications
not: improves focus when you multitask

cards.subject: A study goal
says: turns learn this into a concrete target such as passing level 3 this week
makes progress measurable
is revisited at the end of the week
cards.use: want your effort to have a clear direction
not: is a vague wish to do better

cards.subject: Highlighting only
says: feels like studying but adds little to memory
is weaker than testing yourself
gives a feeling of familiarity without recall
cards.use: catch yourself colouring a page instead of recalling it
not: is the strongest study method

cards.subject: Reading the whole question
says: means finishing the stem before looking at the options
catches words such as NOT and EXCEPT
prevents answering the question you expected
cards.use: feel tempted to jump to the options
not: means skimming the first few words

cards.subject: Reading every option
says: stops you picking the first plausible answer
lets you compare the choices
protects you when two options both look right
cards.use: see an option that looks right straight away
not: means choosing option a every time

cards.subject: Eliminating options
says: narrows the choices by crossing out clearly wrong ones
raises your odds when you are unsure
works well with a distractor that contradicts the question
cards.use: are not sure of the answer
not: means picking the longest option

cards.subject: An absolute word
says: such as always or never makes a statement easy to disprove
is a clue worth checking rather than a rule
tempts you to doubt an option for the wrong reason
cards.use: see an option containing always or never
not: proves an option is correct

cards.subject: A negative question
says: asks which option is NOT true
is easy to misread when rushing
has three true options and one false one
cards.use: read a question with NOT or EXCEPT in it
not: asks which option is true

cards.subject: Keeping your first answer
says: is usually right unless you find a concrete reason to change
is better than switching from vague doubt
does not mean refusing to correct a clear mistake
cards.use: doubt an answer but cannot say why
not: means never reviewing your answers

cards.subject: Pacing
says: means not spending too long on one question
keeps time for the rest of the exam
starts with a sense of the time per question
cards.use: find yourself stuck on one hard question
not: means answering as fast as you can

cards.subject: An educated guess
says: uses elimination first and then picks the most likely option
beats a random pick
draws on partial knowledge
cards.use: cannot recall the answer
not: means choosing at random from all the options

cards.subject: A qualifier word
says: such as first, best or most likely asks for a ranking among true-looking options
changes which answer is correct
is easy to read past
cards.use: read a question asking for the best or first step
not: can be ignored

cards.subject: Answering the question asked
says: means addressing what an open question asks, not everything you know
earns marks under a rubric
keeps a written answer focused
cards.use: are writing an open answer
not: means writing everything you know about the topic

cards.subject: Scenario answer structure
says: states the action, the reason and how you would check it worked
covers the key points of a rubric
stays tied to the situation described
cards.use: face a scenario question and are unsure how to organise the answer
not: means listing every fact you know

cards.subject: Exam anxiety
says: is reduced by slow breathing and by practising under exam conditions
is normal and manageable
eases when you know the format and the pass mark
cards.use: feel your heart racing before an exam
not: proves you are not ready

cards.subject: Honest self-assessment
says: means judging what you actually know, not what you hope
looks for the topics you cannot explain
makes your study time more efficient
cards.use: want to decide what to revise
not: means assuming you know what you have read

cards.subject: The illusion of knowing
says: makes material feel known because it looks familiar
comes from rereading
is exposed when you try to recall without looking
cards.use: read the guide three times and still miss questions
not: comes from testing yourself

cards.subject: Recognition
says: means spotting the right answer when you see it
is easier than recall
is what multiple-choice questions mostly use
cards.use: find an answer easy to spot but hard to produce
not: means producing an answer unprompted

cards.subject: Recall
says: means producing an answer without any prompt
is what a written answer or a real task needs
is harder than recognition
cards.use: must write an answer with no options in front of you
not: means choosing from a list

cards.subject: Calibration
says: compares how confident you feel with how often you are right
improves when you rate confidence before checking
is poor when you are often sure and wrong
cards.use: want to know whether your confidence matches your results
not: means feeling confident about everything

cards.subject: A confidence rating
says: is a quick label such as sure, unsure or guessing made before the answer is shown
separates lucky guesses from knowledge
shows where you are overconfident
cards.use: want to tell guesses from knowledge
not: is made after you see the result

cards.subject: An error log
says: records each miss together with its cause
reveals repeated patterns in your mistakes
guides what to revise next
cards.use: want to find out why you keep losing marks
not: lists only your correct answers

cards.subject: A careless error
says: comes from misreading, not from missing knowledge
is fixed by slowing down rather than studying more
is common with NOT questions
cards.use: missed a question although you knew the topic
not: is fixed by more revision of the topic

cards.subject: A knowledge gap
says: means you did not know the fact or idea
is fixed by targeted review
shows up as the same topic being missed again and again
cards.use: keep missing questions on one topic
not: is fixed by reading the question more slowly

cards.subject: Learning from a failed exam
says: starts with reading which topics you missed
treats the result as information rather than a verdict
leads to a targeted plan before the retake
cards.use: have just failed an exam
not: means retaking at once without reviewing

cards.subject: Comparing with a rival
says: works as a nudge but not as a measure of your own competence
is more useful beside your own progress last week
can discourage you if it becomes the only goal
cards.use: feel behind your rival on the dashboard
not: tells you exactly what you know

cards.subject: Habit stacking
says: attaches a new habit to an existing one
uses a current routine as the cue
could mean doing a drill right after your morning coffee
cards.use: want to build a daily study habit
not: relies on remembering at random

cards.subject: An implementation intention
says: states when and where you will act in an if-then form
beats a vague aim
removes the decision at the moment of action
cards.use: keep saying you will study soon
not: is a promise with no time attached

cards.subject: A minimum session
says: keeps a habit alive on bad days with a tiny version
could be one five-question drill
protects a streak when time is short
cards.use: have a very busy day but want to stay consistent
not: means skipping the day

cards.subject: Never missing twice
says: treats one missed day as normal
treats two missed days as the start of a slide
tells you to restart with a small step
cards.use: missed yesterday and wonder what to do today
not: means making up for a miss with a huge session

cards.subject: Intrinsic motivation
says: comes from interest in the subject itself
lasts longer than a reward
grows when you can see your own progress
cards.use: want a reason to keep learning beyond points
not: comes from badges and prizes

cards.subject: Extrinsic motivation
says: comes from outside rewards such as XP, badges or a deadline
can get you started
fades when the reward stops
cards.use: are driven mainly by points or a due date
not: comes from enjoying the topic

cards.subject: Gamification
says: uses points, streaks and badges to encourage practice
works best when it supports real learning
can backfire when the score becomes the goal
cards.use: wonder why a learning product shows XP and streaks
not: replaces the need to learn

cards.subject: The progress principle
says: says visible small wins are a strong motivator
explains why levels and badges help
is strongest when the progress is real
cards.use: want to keep going when the goal feels far away
not: says only big milestones motivate

cards.subject: A growth mindset
says: treats ability as something that develops with effort
views a failed exam as feedback
makes retaking an exam less threatening
cards.use: feel that you are simply bad at a subject
not: treats ability as fixed at birth

cards.subject: Social accountability
says: makes you more likely to keep commitments you have shared
can come from telling someone your goal
is one idea behind racing a rival or a contest
cards.use: want an outside push to study regularly
not: works best when kept secret

cards.subject: Streak obsession
says: can push you to do a token quest just to keep the number
loses sight of why you are learning
is avoided by remembering the streak is a prompt to learn
cards.use: notice you are doing the minimum only to keep a streak
not: is the best sign of learning

cards.subject: Asking for a new invite
says: is the fix when a link has expired or been used
goes to the person who invited you
is quicker than trying the old link again
cards.use: find that your invite link is not valid
not: means signing up on the home page

cards.subject: Re-reading the study guide
says: is the first move when you keep missing the same topic
points you to the level's syllabus
should be followed by a self-test
cards.use: keep failing questions on one topic
not: replaces trying a drill

cards.subject: Reading drill feedback
says: explains the right answer straight after a drill question
turns a wrong answer into learning
is worth reading even when you were right
cards.use: have just answered a drill question
not: is skipped to save time

cards.subject: A clear problem report
says: says what you did, what you expected and what happened
names the track and level involved
leaves out your password
cards.use: need to ask for help with something that went wrong
not: says only that it does not work

cards.subject: A request for your password
says: should be refused whoever asks
is never needed to fix an account problem
is a warning sign
cards.use: are asked to hand over your password so someone can fix an issue
not: is normal when you ask for help

cards.subject: Not seeing a track
says: can mean the track is not made for customers
is a reason to ask whoever set up your account
does not mean your account is broken
cards.use: cannot find a track a staff colleague mentioned
not: means your progress was deleted

cards.subject: A mistyped email address
says: is a common reason an invite appears not to work
matters because an invite is tied to one address
is solved by asking for a new link with the right address
cards.use: typed your email slightly differently from the invite
not: is ignored by the invite system

cards.subject: Signing in again
says: is a quick check before assuming the site is broken
starts a fresh session
can clear a stale page
cards.use: see a page that will not load properly
not: is the last thing to try

cards.subject: Taking a break
says: restores focus when you are stuck
lets your mind work on the problem in the background
is better than staring at the same question
cards.use: have been stuck on a topic for a long time
not: means giving up for good

qa.q: What score do you need to pass a GGLearn level exam?
qa.why: The pass mark is 80%.

qa.q: How many levels does a GGLearn track have?
qa.why: Every track runs from level 1 (Novice) to level 20 (Titan).

qa.q: You passed level 4 yesterday and want to sit level 6 today. What do you need to do first?
qa.right: Pass level 5, because levels unlock in order
wrong: Nothing, because any level can be taken at any time
Ask your rival to unlock it
Create a second account and start again
qa.why: Levels unlock one after another.

qa.q: Which levels issue a certificate when you pass them?
qa.right: Levels 5, 10, 15 and 20
qa.why: Milestone levels 5, 10, 15 and 20 each issue a certificate.

qa.q: What is the certificate for level 10 called?
qa.right: Practitioner
qa.why: Foundation is level 5, Practitioner level 10, Expert level 15 and Titan level 20.

qa.q: You completed a quest on Monday, nothing on Tuesday or Wednesday, and you open GGLearn on Thursday. What is your streak?
qa.right: Zero, because a streak must end today or yesterday
wrong: Three, because you were active this week
Two, because the missed days are forgiven
qa.why: A streak counts consecutive days ending today or yesterday.

qa.q: You completed quests on Saturday, Sunday and Monday. It is Tuesday morning and you have not done a quest yet. What does your streak show?
qa.right: Three days, which stays alive until today ends
wrong: Zero, because nothing is done today
One, because only the latest day counts
It resets automatically when you log in
qa.why: The streak runs to yesterday and survives until a full day passes with no quest.

qa.q: Which daily quest earns the most XP?
qa.right: Finishing a level exam (+40)
qa.why: Exam +40, drill +30, study guide +20.

qa.q: You read the study guide and answer a drill today. How much XP is that in total?
qa.right: 50 XP
qa.why: 20 for the study guide plus 30 for the drill.

qa.q: A rival has earned 600 XP on the scale GGLearn uses. What level does that equal?
qa.right: Level 4
qa.why: 150 XP equals one level, so 600 divided by 150 is 4.

qa.q: Your invite link says it is not valid. What is the most likely reason?
qa.right: It has expired or been used, so you should ask for a new one
wrong: Links only work on mobile phones
qa.why: An invite is single-use and valid for 7 days.

qa.q: You forward your invite link to a colleague so they can join. What is the problem?
qa.right: The link is single-use and tied to one email address, so they need their own invite
wrong: Invites can only be forwarded once
Colleagues can only join through a contest
Nothing: any number of people can use one link
qa.why: Each invite belongs to one email address.

qa.q: How long must a GGLearn password be?
qa.right: At least 8 characters
wrong: At least 16 characters with a symbol
qa.why: Passwords are 8 characters or more.

qa.q: Which photo can you upload to your profile?
qa.right: A JPEG, PNG or WebP image up to 300 KB
wrong: Only a PNG up to 100 KB
A GIF or JPEG up to 1 MB
qa.why: A profile photo is optional and limited in type and size.

qa.q: You have never played in a public contest. Who can see your profile photo?
qa.right: Signed-in colleagues, but not strangers
qa.why: Strangers see a photo only if you play in a public contest.

qa.q: A friend says join this public contest, it is easy. What should you know before joining?
qa.right: Joining requires consent that your name, photo and progress become public
wrong: Your password becomes visible to others
You must pay an entry fee to GGLearn
qa.why: Public contests show your name, photo and progress, so you must consent.

qa.q: Two players both reached a contest goal. How does the ranking decide who is ahead?
qa.right: Whoever reached the goal first
wrong: Whoever started at a higher level
qa.why: Ranking goes to who reached the goal first, then levels gained, then XP in the window.

qa.q: An expert starting at level 12 and a beginner starting at level 1 enter a contest to gain 3 levels. Why is it fair?
qa.right: Progress is measured as levels gained, not the level you already hold
wrong: Experts are not allowed to win
qa.why: Growth, not starting level, is what the contest measures.

qa.q: A contest entry is labelled as simulated. What does that entry do?
qa.right: Follows a fixed daily XP schedule and does not study or answer questions
wrong: Answers questions faster than a human
Is a real learner who asked to be hidden
Is controlled by the organiser answering exams
qa.why: Bots are simulated and labelled as such.

qa.q: A contest organiser promises a cash prize. Who pays the winners?
qa.right: The organiser, because GGLearn never holds or moves money
wrong: Nobody, since prizes are not allowed
qa.why: Prizes are optional and arranged by the organiser.

qa.q: A colleague who was not invited tries to open a private contest. What do they see?
qa.right: A not-found page
wrong: A request to pay to join
qa.why: Only the organiser, invited people and members can open a private contest.

qa.q: How long can a contest run?
qa.right: From 1 to 90 days
qa.why: A contest has a deadline of 1 to 90 days.

qa.q: What is the goal of a contest?
qa.right: Gain a set number of levels, from 1 to 20, before the deadline
wrong: Pass one exam with a perfect score
qa.why: A contest is a race to gain levels.

qa.q: You think you left yourself signed in on a shared computer. What should you do?
qa.right: Use Sign out everywhere to end your session on every device
wrong: Wait for the session to expire on its own
Close the browser and hope for the best
qa.why: Sign out everywhere ends all your sessions.

qa.q: Which is the strongest password habit?
qa.right: A long, unique passphrase kept in a password manager
wrong: Your name plus your birth year
One strong password reused on every site
A short password written on a note under the keyboard
qa.why: Unique, long passwords limit the damage when a site is breached.

qa.q: You get an email saying your account locks in one hour unless you click a link and confirm your password. What do you do?
qa.right: Do not click; go to the site directly and check there
wrong: Click the link quickly and enter your password
Reply with your password so they can check it
Forward the email to colleagues first
qa.why: Urgency and a request for your password are phishing signs.

qa.q: What does the placement check do?
qa.right: Finds the level you already know so you can start there instead of level 1
wrong: Ranks you against all other learners
qa.why: It saves you repeating what you already know.

qa.q: You answer every placement question correctly. What is the highest level you can be placed at?
qa.right: Level 15
qa.why: Placement never goes past level 15; higher levels are earned by exam.

qa.q: You score 7 out of 10 on a level exam. What happens?
qa.right: The level stays locked and you can try again with a fresh draw of questions
wrong: You are removed from the track
You pass because 7 is a majority
qa.why: The pass mark is 80%, and a failed exam can be retaken at once.

qa.q: An exam asks 10 questions. What is the smallest number you must answer correctly to pass?
You have two weeks to pass a level exam. Which plan is best?
qa.right: Short daily sessions of drills with a review of every miss
wrong: Reread the study guide once the night before
One six-hour session at the weekend
Highlight the whole guide and stop there
qa.why: Spaced retrieval practice plus review of mistakes builds lasting memory.

qa.q: Which activity is retrieval practice?
qa.right: Answering a question from memory before checking the answer
wrong: Copying the syllabus out by hand
qa.why: Retrieval means pulling the answer out of memory.

qa.q: Which schedule uses spaced practice?
qa.right: 20 minutes on Monday, Wednesday and Friday
wrong: Six 10-minute blocks back to back on Friday
Reading everything once on the night before
qa.why: Spacing spreads the same study across several days.

qa.q: Studying topics A, B and C by mixing them within one session is called what?
qa.right: Interleaving
qa.why: Interleaving mixes topics instead of finishing one at a time.

qa.q: You reread the study guide three times and it all feels familiar, but you still miss exam-style questions. What is the likely cause?
qa.right: Familiarity is being mistaken for recall; test yourself instead
wrong: You need to read it a fourth time
qa.why: The illusion of knowing comes from recognising rather than recalling.

qa.q: A question asks which option is NOT true. Which option do you choose?
qa.right: The one statement that is false
wrong: The statement that is most true
qa.why: On a NOT question three options are true and one is false.

qa.q: You are unsure, and one option says always while another says usually. What is a sound move?
qa.right: Treat the absolute option with suspicion and test it with a counter-example
wrong: Always pick the option with always in it
Ignore both and choose at random
qa.why: Absolute words are easy to disprove, but they are a clue, not a rule.

qa.q: You are unsure of an answer but can rule out two of the four options. What next?
qa.right: Choose between the remaining two using what you know
wrong: Pick at random from all four
Change to the option you ruled out
qa.why: Elimination improves your odds.

qa.q: Near the end you doubt an earlier answer but cannot say why. What should you do?
qa.right: Keep it unless you find a concrete reason to change
wrong: Change it, because doubt means it is wrong
Change it to a different option at random
qa.why: Vague doubt is a weak reason to switch.

qa.q: An open question asks Explain why spaced practice helps. Which answer scores best against a rubric?
qa.right: Reviewing just as memory fades strengthens it, so retention lasts longer than with cramming
wrong: Spaced practice is practice that is spaced, as the name says
qa.why: A good answer covers the key points rather than repeating the question.

qa.q: A scenario question describes a colleague whose invite link has expired. How should you structure the answer?
qa.right: Say what you would do, why, and how you would check it worked
wrong: List every fact about invites you know
Argue that the scenario is unrealistic
qa.why: Action, reason and check cover the points a rubric looks for.

qa.q: You missed five questions: three because you misread NOT, and two because you did not know the topic. What is the right response?
qa.right: Slow down on NOT questions and review the two topics
wrong: Study all five topics from scratch
Do nothing; five misses is normal
qa.why: Different causes need different fixes.

qa.q: You rated yourself sure on 10 answers and 5 were wrong. What does this show?
qa.right: You are overconfident, so check your answers more carefully
qa.why: Calibration compares confidence with accuracy.

qa.q: Which statement reflects honest self-assessment before an exam?
qa.right: I can explain each topic without notes except the second one, which I will review
wrong: I have read everything so I must know it
I will recognise the answers when I see them
Other people pass this so I will too
qa.why: Honest assessment names what you can and cannot recall.

qa.q: You missed a day yesterday. What is the best response today?
qa.right: Do a small quest today so you never miss twice
wrong: Wait until next week to restart
Give up on the streak for good
Try to do five days of quests today
qa.why: One miss is normal; the aim is not to miss twice.

qa.q: You have a very bad day and only 10 minutes. What keeps your habit going?
qa.right: One five-question drill
qa.why: A minimum session protects the habit.

qa.q: At 11:58 pm you do a quest only to keep your streak and learn nothing. What is the lesson?
qa.right: A streak is a prompt to learn, so aim for real study even on a small scale
wrong: Quests should never be done late
qa.why: The streak serves the learning, not the other way round.

qa.q: A colleague on a staff account mentions a track you cannot find on your customer account. Why?
qa.right: Customer accounts only see tracks made for customers
wrong: You must pay extra to see it
Tracks appear only after you pass level 5
qa.why: Customers only ever see customer tracks.

qa.q: The dashboard shows a required track as overdue. What should you do?
qa.right: Work on it first, because required learning has a due date
wrong: Wait for your rival to finish it
qa.why: Required learning is listed under Required for you with due dates.

qa.q: When is the study guide most useful?
qa.right: Before a level exam, to see the syllabus and flip cards
wrong: After you have passed the track
Only when you have failed twice
qa.why: The study guide prepares you for the level.

qa.q: You have just passed level 3 of a track. Which levels can your drill questions come from?
qa.right: Only levels 1 to 3
qa.why: Drills draw only from levels you have already passed.

qa.q: Which message is most likely to get you help quickly?
qa.right: On the level 4 exam, I pressed Submit and saw a blank page; I am on a laptop
wrong: Here is my password so you can look
qa.why: A clear problem report says what you did and what happened, without secrets.

qa.q: How can an employer check that a GGLearn certificate is genuine?
qa.right: Use its public code at /cert/ followed by the code
qa.why: Every certificate has a public code that can be verified.

qa.q: How are written answers marked?
qa.right: Against a reference answer and a rubric of key points
qa.why: Written answers are graded against a reference answer and rubric.

qa.q: Why does struggling to recall an answer help long-term memory?
qa.right: Effortful retrieval strengthens the memory more than easy rereading
wrong: It does not; easy study is always better
It slows forgetting only while you are awake
It matters only for multiple-choice tests
qa.why: Desirable difficulty improves retention.

qa.q: You have two hours before bed the night before a big exam. Which choice supports memory best?
qa.right: Review for part of the time, then get a full night of sleep
wrong: Skip sleep and rely on memory
Sleep four hours and study again
qa.why: Sleep consolidates what you have just learned.
